### Load packages

```{r load-packages, message = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
```


# Questioning data visualisations

## Image 1

```{r echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/Speaking-the-world.jpg")
```

The first 9 rows of the data are all the same width, but because Chinese is so big, it has a different width to the others, making it difficult to comprehend how widely spoken Chinese is. It would probably be better to do this box plot vertically and have them all the same width to show just how many people speak Chinese in comparison to all the other languages.




## Image 2

```{r echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/rose-pop-density-total-area-bw.jpg")
```

Provides a nice pie chart visual but fails to show any actual quantitatuve data, meaning people have to guess or estimate countries population density and total area. This would probably be better as a box plot rather than a pie chart as well.




## Image 3

```{r echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/life-expectancy-rule-of-law.png")
```

The scatter diagram is extremely crowded and difficult to distinguish between each data point. There is also no key to inform the reader what the opacity or colours mean and again there is no scale on the axis so readers are forced to infer what each point's value is.




## Image 4

```{r echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/global-income-dist.PNG")
```

Quite a difficult graph to visually understand. Whilst it makes good use of colours to distinguish between countries, it is quite a cramped graph. It does include data on the x axis, which is informative, but none on the y (although it is not really required as the area under the graph represents the regional size of the population)



# Data Visualization for Halloween 

Ensure that you have the following two lines of code at the top of `lab-05.Rmd` to make the commands available to you.

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

# Install that package first 
# install.packages("fivethirtyeight")
library(fivethirtyeight)
```


```{r}
candy_df <- candy_rankings
glimpse(candy_df)
```


## Exercise 1

How many observations and variables are in this dataset?
Did you identify the type of variables, remember that this detail is crucial to create which kind of data visualization in general. 

In the data, there are 13x85 = 1105 obseravtions and there are 85 variables (some character, logical and double)

# Data viz - One variable at a time

Just to use the logical variables as categories, run the following code chunk first!

```{r}
candy_df <- candy_df %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.logical), as_factor))
```

## Exercise 2

Complete the following code to get the data viz to represent "how many candies contain caramel via bar plot". Fill in the blanks, remove the # symbol in front of your code and the execute the code chunk via green play button.

```{r}
ggplot(candy_rankings, aes(x = caramel)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    x = "Candy type",
    y = "Contains caramel"
  )
```

## Exercise 3

Now look at a numerical variable, such as `winpercent`. Create an histogram for this variable using ggplot2 functions below. Include informative x and y labels and a title, as a good practice.

```{r}
ggplot(candy_rankings, aes(x = winpercent)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
    labs(
        x = "Win percentage",
        y = "Candy"
    )


```


# Data viz - more than one variable

## Exercise 4

How about using the both variables; chocolate vs winpercent? Run the following incomplete code snippet to get a faceted visualization.

Fill in the blanks, remove the # symbol in front of your code and the execute the code chunk via green play button.

```{r}
# Your code here
ggplot(candy_df, aes(x = winpercent, fill = caramel)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  facet_wrap(~chocolate)

```


- Consider adding the `fill = caramel` within the aes() vs. geom_histogram(), what do you get? 

## Exercise 5

Create a visualization that examines the relationship between a candy’s win percentage and whether it contains chocolate. Include x and y labels and a title. Describe any relationship you see.

```{r}
ggplot(candy_df, aes(x = winpercent)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~chocolate)

```

- Consider the similar pair by replacing chocolate with caramel, fruity and compare their results. 
- Also include summary statistics details for this discussion by using the calculation below: 

```{r}
candy_rankings %>%
  group_by(chocolate) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_win = mean(winpercent),
    median_win = median(winpercent)
  )
```


## Exercise 6

Do more expensive candies win more often? Make a scatterplot of pricepercent (x) against winpercent (y). Describe their relationship.  

There is no obvious relationship between pricepercent and winpercent.

```{r}
ggplot(candy_df, aes(x = pricepercent, y = winpercent, colour = chocolate)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(
        x = "Price percentage",
        y = "Win percentage"
    ) + 
  facet_wrap(~bar)

```


- Add `color = chocolate` to add a third variable to the created visualization
- How to facet this by using another categorical variable such as `bar`? 


## Exercise 7

Are chocolate candies more likely to be candy bars? Make a filled bar plot with chocolate on the x-axis and fill = bar. Describe what you see.

Chocolate bars are much more likely to be a candy bar as shown by the graph because on the TRUE side of the x axis, there is a much greater blue bar than on the left side, showing chocolate is more likely to be a bar.

```{r}
ggplot(candy_df, aes(x = chocolate, fill = bar)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    x = "Chocolate",
  )


```
